title: Cultural Humility, Diversity, Accessibility, and Bias Awareness

unit.title: Program Orientation, Professionalism, and Healthcare Roles

sections.learningObjectives:
- Define cultural humility and distinguish it from cultural competence, and explain its role in patient care.
- Recognize accessibility needs and accommodations for patients with disabilities and apply effective communication supports.
- Identify unconscious bias, stereotypes, and discrimination and describe their impact on equitable care.
- Apply respectful, non-stigmatizing, person-centered language and communication in medical office settings.
- Demonstrate non-discriminatory, equitable care practices within the medical office assistant scope of practice.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Cultural humility is like being a respectful guest who keeps learning about a friend's family traditions instead of assuming one visit taught you everything. You stay curious and keep asking kindly.

### Question 2

Think of 'competence' like a trophy you might win once, while 'humility' is like practicing a sport for life. Humility says you keep improving and never claim to know it all.

### Question 3

Imagine a friend who doesn't eat a certain food because of their family's beliefs. You wouldn't argue they are wrong; you'd respect their choice and let them know their options.

### Question 4

If you made a list saying 'all kids love pizza,' you'd be wrong about the kids who don't. People in a group are all different, so a one-size list can't tell you about one person.

### Question 5

If you catch yourself thinking something unfair about a group, the brave thing is to notice it and change, like admitting you were wrong about a friend and treating them better after.

### Question 6

Instead of guessing what a guest wants at a party, a good host asks. Being curious and asking is the polite and smart way to help people.

### Question 7

Cultural humility means always being willing to learn more about people, like a student who never stops asking good questions.

### Question 8

If you meet a new classmate, the best way to learn about them is to ask them, not to guess from rumors. Asking kindly is respectful.

### Question 9

If a friend says no thank you to a snack, you respect their choice and tell the host, rather than making them take it. Patients get to make their own health choices.

### Question 10

It's like being a lifelong learner of people: you keep paying attention, asking, and being kind every single day.

### Question 11

In a classroom, the teacher knows more than the student, and a good teacher uses that kindly instead of bossing. Health workers should use their position with care and respect.

### Question 12

You wouldn't say you're 'done' learning to be a good friend after one conversation. Being kind and understanding people is a forever kind of learning.

### Question 13

Respecting someone's background is like respecting a friend's favorite holiday even if you don't celebrate it. You can be kind and honor it without it being your own.

### Question 14

If a friend can't come to your party at a certain time because of a family tradition, you'd pick another time instead of scolding them. Respect means finding a way that works.

### Question 15

If someone speaks another language, the fair thing is to get a helper who speaks both languages well, not to shout or leave things out.

### Question 16

If a classmate asks to be called by a nickname, you use it. Calling people what they ask to be called is just polite.

### Question 17

People are different in lots of ways, like the foods they eat, the languages they speak, and the abilities they have. Diversity means all those differences together.

### Question 18

If someone keeps talking for your friend, you'd gently ask your friend directly, because they should get to speak for themselves.

### Question 19

If a friend tells you about a home remedy they use, the smart thing is to listen and tell the doctor, not to pretend it doesn't matter.

### Question 20

Being a good teammate means being excited to meet all kinds of people, not only people just like you.

### Question 21

If your friend wants their family around for support during a hard time, you let them, while still making sure your friend's own wishes count most.

### Question 22

If a school test needs you to eat breakfast but a friend is fasting, the helper finds another day rather than forcing the friend to break their fast.

### Question 23

Different families have different rules about eye contact, just like some people like hugs and some don't. A good helper notices what makes someone comfortable.

### Question 24

Everyone deserves to be treated like a person, not a label. Good helpers ask people what they need instead of guessing.

### Question 25

If someone asks to be helped by a certain person and the office can make it work, the kind thing is to try to make it happen.

### Question 26

If someone makes fun of how a person talks, the right thing is to say that's not okay, not to laugh or pass it on.

### Question 27

Accessibility means making sure everyone can get in, understand, and be helped, like building a ramp so a friend in a wheelchair can come to your house.

### Question 28

Making things accessible means giving people the tools they need, like big letters for a friend who can't see small print or a signer for a friend who is Deaf.

### Question 29

The polite thing is to ask a person how they'd like to talk and give them what they need, like a sign language helper, instead of guessing.

### Question 30

If a friend in a wheelchair visits, you make sure there's a clear path and a place they can sit, instead of saying it's too hard.

### Question 31

If a friend can't read the small words, you read them out loud or make the letters bigger so they can fill it in themselves.

### Question 32

When you meet someone, you talk to them, not just to the person beside them. Everyone deserves to be spoken to directly and kindly.

### Question 33

The law is like a school rule that says every student gets the help they need to join in, and the school can't charge them for it.

### Question 34

Effective communication means both people truly understand each other, like using a translator so a game's rules are clear to everyone.

### Question 35

If a friend's wheelchair can't fit through your door, you'd find another way in and tell an adult to fix the door, not just ignore it.

### Question 36

Moving someone safely is like lifting a heavy box with a friend and a cart instead of doing it alone and hurting your back.

### Question 37

A reasonable accommodation is a fair change that helps someone take part, like moving a game to a table a friend can reach.

### Question 38

A service animal is like a helper with a job to do, so you let it stay with its person and don't distract it while it's working.

### Question 39

A nod is like saying 'okay' to be polite, but you want to be sure a friend really understood the directions, so you show them a map too.

### Question 40

Accessibility isn't just about getting in the door; it's about being able to understand and take part the whole time.

### Question 41

If a friend needs a translator for an important meeting, you book the translator ahead of time so everything goes smoothly.

### Question 42

Unconscious bias is like a shortcut your brain takes automatically, like grabbing the same snack without thinking. You didn't plan it, but it still happens.

### Question 43

Bias is like wearing slightly tinted glasses you forgot you have on; it changes what you see even when you don't mean it to.

### Question 44

Thinking all grandparents are bad with phones is like thinking all kids hate vegetables; it's a guess, not a fact about each person.

### Question 45

To avoid unfair shortcuts, you pause and follow the same checklist for everyone, like measuring ingredients instead of guessing.

### Question 46

If you notice you explain the rules fully to some friends but rush others, the fair fix is to explain fully to everyone.

### Question 47

One is like bumping into someone by accident; the other is pushing on purpose. Both can hurt, but only one was planned.

### Question 48

A stereotype is like saying 'all dogs chase cats' — it might be true for some, but it's not true about every single dog.

### Question 49

Instead of guessing from what you've heard, you ask the person right in front of you what they need. That's the fair way.

### Question 50

Saying 'those kids never do their homework' isn't fair to the ones who do. The kind response is to think about each person's real situation.

### Question 51

Writing down exactly what you saw without calling someone names, like 'spilled the milk' instead of 'is clumsy,' keeps things fair.

### Question 52

Everyone has blind spots, like a driver who can't see everything behind the car. Being aware of them keeps everyone safe.

### Question 53

You can't tell how much money someone has by where they live, so you ask them instead of guessing.

### Question 54

The best way to break a bad habit is to notice it and use the same fair routine every time, not to pretend it isn't there.

### Question 55

There are rules that say a doctor's office can't treat people unfairly because of things like their skin color, where they're from, or a disability.

### Question 56

Non-discrimination means everyone gets treated just as well as everyone else, like a teacher who calls on every student fairly.

### Question 57

If someone is being treated unfairly because of where they're from, the right move is to tell a trusted adult or boss, not to look away.

### Question 58

If a friend says they were treated unfairly, you listen and get help, not tell them it's all in their head.

### Question 59

A real doctor choice is based on what's medically best; refusing someone because of their religion is just unfair and not allowed.

### Question 60

The office must provide a translator for free, like a school providing a helper so a new student can understand class.

### Question 61

The office should offer a free translator, like a museum giving visitors a free audio guide in their own language.

### Question 62

Making a patient bring their own helper is like asking them to bring their own doctor; the office should provide what's needed for good care.

### Question 63

Equity is like giving everyone the size of ladder they need to see over a fence, not the same ladder for a tall person and a short person.

### Question 64

Unfairness can happen by accident or on purpose, and it can come from one person or from how a whole system is set up.

### Question 65

Person-first language says the person comes first, like 'a kid with a broken arm' instead of 'the broken-arm kid.'

### Question 66

Saying 'a person with diabetes' is polite; calling them 'a diabetic' is like naming them only by their illness.

### Question 67

A wheelchair is a helpful tool, like glasses. We say a person 'uses glasses,' not that they're 'trapped in glasses.'

### Question 68

Non-stigmatizing language means not calling people mean names or labeling them by one thing about them.

### Question 69

We describe a health problem with its real medical name instead of calling someone a hurtful nickname.

### Question 70

Calling someone 'noncompliant' is like calling a kid 'bad' instead of finding out why they didn't finish their homework.

### Question 71

It's the difference between 'a person who is tall' and 'a tall person' — one focuses on the person, the other on the trait.

### Question 72

Words are like tone of voice; even if you do the right thing, saying it meanly can hurt. Kind words make people want to come back.

### Question 73

If you call a friend by the wrong name, you say 'sorry' and use the right name next time. It's that simple.

### Question 74

Instead of calling someone 'difficult,' you write exactly what they did, like 'asked three times for help,' which is fair and true.

### Question 75

Calling someone 'non-compliant' is like calling them 'lazy' when they might just need help; it blames instead of understanding.

### Question 76

Person-centered care means thinking about the whole person and what matters to them, like helping a friend with their real goals, not just their one problem.

### Question 77

Health equity is like making sure every runner starts at the same line and has the shoes they need, so the race is fair for everyone.

### Question 78

If a friend can't get a ride to practice, you help find one instead of saying they don't care about the team.

### Question 79

If a friend can't afford their medicine, you tell the doctor and help find a program that helps pay, never tell them to skip or split pills on their own.

### Question 80

Equity is like giving each student the kind of help they need to understand a lesson, instead of reading the same page to everyone and hoping for the best.

### Question 81

Where you live, whether you have a ride, and how much money your family has can all affect how healthy you are—those are the 'conditions of your life.'

### Question 82

If a friend keeps missing practice because of a job, you find a time that works instead of calling them unreliable.

### Question 83

Being fair means noticing when someone needs extra help and giving it, like helping a shorter friend reach the high shelf.

### Question 84

To be sure a friend understood directions, you explain simply and ask them to say it back in their own words.

### Question 85

If one friend needs glasses and another needs a hearing aid, giving both of them the same pair of glasses helps only one. Fair means giving each what they need.
